questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with several days of fevers, rigors, and chest pain. She was an intravenous drug user, dependent on heroin. She had no other medical history. Physical exam revealed a regurgitant systolic heart murmur. Investigations: Blood cultures: Staphylococcus aureus, susceptible to methicillin Transthoracic echocardiogram: poor visualization of valves due to body habitus.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin This patient has MSSA bacteremia, and there should be some concern that she may also have endocarditis. According to the guidelines, recommended agents in this circumstance would include cefazolin or an antistaphylococcal penicillin (nafcillin or oxacillin). Alternative agents may be employed based on individual circumstances (e.g., vancomycin in the setting of β-lactam allergy).

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man was diagnosed with endocarditis caused by viridans streptococcus. He had no known drug allergies. Pending availability of the minimum inhibitory concentration of the organism for penicillin, the patient was initiated on ceftriaxone IV plus gentamicin IV . Investigations: Serum creatinine 0.55 mg/dL Total white cell count 14.5 ×109/L Normal liver function tests
questions.lead_in: What gentamicin serum concentration is in the desired range?
questions.explanation: Trough concentration of 0.8 μg/mL The desired gentamicin serum trough concentration range for synergistic therapy of gram-positive infections is <1 μg/mL, in order to preserve activity and minimize risk of aminoglycoside toxicity. The desired gentamicin peak concentration range for synergistic treatment of endocarditis caused by viridans streptococcus is 3–4 μg/mL. When used for treatment of serious gram-negative infections, a typical gentamicin peak concentration range to target is 4–10 μg/ mL.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q2

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of intermittent fevers and pain in his right collar bone. He was an active intravenous drug user, using heroin and cocaine regularly. He had previously cleared hepatitis C infection. He was not on a methadone program. He had no known drug allergies. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 50 ml/min ALT 241 U/L 4/4 blood cultures positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus Echocardiogram: valvular vegetations and insufficiency involving both the mitral and aortic valve CT chest: pulmonary lesions consistent with septic emboli and fluid collection and bony erosions of the right sternoclavicular joint
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin This patient has infective endocarditis (IE) due to MSSA with evidence of septic complications. Ideal therapy for native valve endocarditis (NVE) due to MSSA includes oxacillin, nafcillin, or cefazolin. Baseline abnormalities in his LFTs mean that avoiding oxacillin is advisable, as it can frequently be associated with hepatotoxicity, and instead use cefazolin give its proven efficacy and safe adverse effects profile. Although vancomycin is an alternative treatment for patients with MSSA IE intolerant to penicillins and cephalosporins, beta-lactam therapy is preferred whenever feasible and should be selected over vancomycin. There is no role for rifampin or aminoglycoside therapy in NVE due to MSSA.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q7

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of lumbar back pain and night sweats. He was known to have a previous abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair and bladder cancer surgically removed and followed by intravesical BCG immunotherapy. He was born in the United States and was stationed in Vietnam for almost 2 years, but was TST negative while in the military. Abdominal CT showed a 2-cm paraaortic mass contiguous to the AAA mesh concerning for vascular leak. An open surgical repair was undertaken, and biopsies sent for histology. Investigations: Histopathology of the tissue showed granulomatous inflammation TST: positive at 11 mm Interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) negative
questions.lead_in: What agent should be avoided as part as the treatment regimen?
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide BCG is a live-attenuated strain derived from Mycobacterium bovis, both of which are intrinsically resistant to PZA; thus this agent is not indicated as part of the treatment regimen of disseminated BCG disease. QuantiFERON-TB Gold is negative in this case; IGRA tests are based on detection of a T-cell immune response to TB antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP- 10) encoded by genes in the region of difference-1 (RD1), which is present in M. tuberculosis complex, but absent in M. bovis, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), and most nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q32

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented with fatigue, subjective fever and chills, and poor appetite. He had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and CKD stage 4. He had no known drug allergies. On examination he was found to have a new diastolic murmur. He was started empirically on vancomycin. Investigations: 4/4 blood cultures positive for fully sensitive Enterococcus faecalis Echocardiogram: a 5 mm vegetation of the aortic valve Creatinine clearance 15 mL/min
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone For patients with enterococcal endocarditis with susceptible strains the preferred treatment regimens include ampicillin or penicillin G as these are rapidly cidal agents. For patients with normal renal function these agents should be combined with 2 weeks of aminoglycoside such as gentamicin. In patients with contraindications to aminoglycosides, an alternate regimen of ampicillin and ceftriaxone should be used. Linezolid and daptomycin should be reserved for patients with resistant enterococci not amenable to treatment with rapidly cidal beta-lactams. Vancomycin should be reserved for patients with penicillin-resistant enterococci, and beta-lactams should be used whenever possible. In this patient with a very limited creatinine clearance, vancomycin should also be avoided to prevent further damage to his renal function.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q16

questions.question: Early surgical management of infective endocarditis.

parts.text: List six indications for early surgical management in infective endocarditis.

parts_raw.text: 6 indications for early surgical management with IE

questions.model_answer: (1) Congestive heart failure from valvular dysfunction (severe aortic or mitral regurgitation, valve perforation or dehiscence). (2) Perivalvular extension of infection: annular or aortic root abscess, fistula, or new heart block/conduction delay. (3) Uncontrolled infection: persistently positive blood cultures or persistent fever beyond 5-7 days of appropriate therapy. (4) Organism unlikely to be cured medically: fungal endocarditis, highly resistant gram-negative bacilli or Pseudomonas left-sided IE, or highly aminoglycoside-resistant enterococci. (5) Recurrent systemic embolism with a persistent or enlarging vegetation, or a large (>10 mm) mobile vegetation with severe valvular regurgitation. (6) Prosthetic valve endocarditis, particularly early PVE, Staphylococcus aureus PVE, or PVE with valve dehiscence/obstruction.
questions.beyond_mandell: AHA 2015 and ESC 2015 IE guidelines give the formal early-surgery indications (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, prevention of embolism); Mandell's supplied pages state only the general principle plus organism-specific indications.

parts.text: Why does the laboratory report only high-level susceptibility?
What therapeutic consequence does high-level aminoglycoside resistance have?
What is the mechanism of high-level aminoglycoside resistance in enterococci?

parts_raw.text: Why does the laboratory report only high level susceptibility?
b) What therapeutic consequence does high-level aminoglycoside resistance have?
c) What is the mechanism of high level aminoglycoside resistance in Enterococci?

questions.model_answer:
a) All enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides, so low-level results are not clinically meaningful; only high-level resistance (HLR) testing predicts whether the synergistic effect with a cell-wall agent is preserved.
b) High-level resistance to both gentamicin and streptomycin abolishes the synergistic bactericidal effect of an aminoglycoside combined with a beta-lactam (or vancomycin); the aminoglycoside can no longer be used for synergy, so a double beta-lactam regimen (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone) should be used instead.
c) Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes: HLR to gentamicin is mostly due to the bifunctional enzyme AAC(6′)-Ie-APH(2″)-Ia; HLR to streptomycin is due to 30S ribosomal subunit mutations or a streptomycin adenylyltransferase.

cohort_answer.text: Only high-level resistance reported: Don't report low-level resistance since all enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides; loss of synergism with beta lactams/vanco if high-level AG resistance present. Therapeutic consequence: Can no longer use AG for synergy with beta-lactam/vanco against enterococcus, if used will lead to clinical failure/higher relapse. Mechanism: AG-modifying enzymes (N-acetylation, O-nucleotidylation, O-phosphorylation) alter the drug so it can no longer bind the 30s ribosome subunit.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Dental plaque-related disease: gingivitis/periodontitis and dental abscess. (2) Native valve infective endocarditis (vegetation). (3) Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection in cystic fibrosis. (4) Chronic otitis media with effusion (also chronic rhinosinusitis, chronic osteomyelitis, chronic diabetic foot ulcer).
b) (1) Poor antibiotic penetration through the exopolysaccharide matrix, which can also bind or inactivate the drug and creates an acidic, anaerobic microenvironment. (2) Organisms are metabolically dormant/slow-growing in stationary phase with heterogeneous gene expression (persister cells), so cell wall-active and other agents that require active growth are ineffective; the matrix also impairs phagocyte and antibody access.
c) (1) Rifampin is highly lipid soluble, penetrates the biofilm and phagocytes, and reaches high intra-biofilm concentrations; it is active at acid pH and against slowly replicating or metabolically dormant staphylococci. (2) It acts by a different target (DNA-dependent RNA polymerase), giving bactericidal synergy with cell wall-active agents, sterilizing the adherent population and preventing new biofilm formation; it must always be combined with a partner drug to prevent emergence of resistance.
questions.beyond_mandell: Biofilm biology is not covered in the supplied pages; answer is from standard sources (Mandell's device-infection and staphylococcal chapters).

cohort_answer.text: Infections without foreign material: Dental infections (gingivitis, dental abscess); IE native valve; CF patients and PNA; Chronic otitis media; Diabetic foot ulcer. Resistance reasons: Antibiotics unable to penetrate biofilm; Bacteria may replicate more slowly/be in stationary phase and less susceptible; Biofilm matrix may complex with/deactivate drug, can be too acidic; Organisms exist in distinct populations/growth stages with heterogeneous gene expression. Rifampin mechanisms: Active against metabolically dormant Staphylococci; Penetrates biofilms efficiently (lipid soluble) producing higher intra-biofilm concentrations; Active in acid environment; Prevents biofilm formation within minutes; Different mechanism than beta-lactams (inhibits RNA synthesis), providing synergy, bactericidal.

questions.model_answer:
a) Because all enterococci have intrinsic low-level aminoglycoside resistance; only high-level resistance testing determines whether the synergistic bactericidal effect of an aminoglycoside plus a cell-wall agent is retained (HLR abolishes synergy).
b) The bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6′)-Ie-APH(2″)-Ia, which enzymatically inactivates gentamicin (and confers HLR to all aminoglycosides except streptomycin).
c) Streptomycin requires serum drug-level monitoring (evaluation of levels is strongly recommended) and carries a higher risk of (often irreversible) ototoxicity; high-level streptomycin resistance also arises by a separate mechanism, so it must be tested independently.

cohort_answer.text:
Why test HLR to Genta: Synergistic activity between cell wall active agents and aminoglycoside is not possible in the setting of high level resistance to Gentamicin. All have low level resistance.
High-level resistance mechanism: Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes – enzyme inactivation
Why Streptomycin less preferable: AHA guidelines: Advantage: less nephrotoxic than gentamicin. Disadvantage: no published studies comparing the efficacy of regimens containing streptomycin or gentamicin; lack of familiarity among clinicians with streptomycin; higher risk of ototoxicity, which may not be reversible; drug availability limitations; most laboratories do not routinely perform serum streptomycin assays; may not have access to a clinical pharmacist to assist in dosing adjustments.

parts_raw.text: In patients who have S. aureus bacteremia, list 5 reasons to do a TEE if the TTE is negative.

questions.model_answer: (1) Persisting high clinical suspicion of IE (a negative TTE does not exclude IE; TEE sensitivity ~95% vs 60-65%). (2) Prosthetic valve or intracardiac device/hardware. (3) Technically inadequate/nondiagnostic TTE (obesity, COPD, chest-wall deformity). (4) Suspicion of intracardiac or perivalvular complication (abscess, new AV block, valve perforation). questions.model_answer: a) Differential: (1) Acute HIV (retroviral syndrome) - fever, rash, splenomegaly; consider HIV-associated opportunistic causes (Bartonella henselae/quintana, disseminated salmonellosis). (2) Infective endocarditis (injection-related, typically S. aureus; right-sided) with embolic/immunologic phenomena. (3) Secondary syphilis (diffuse rash including palms/soles). (4) Acute viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV) or mononucleosis-type infection (EBV, CMV, acute toxoplasmosis). (5) Other: disseminated gonococcemia, rickettsial infection, acute HBV serum-sickness; non-infectious mimics (drug reaction, Still disease, SLE). b) (1) Admit; standard/contact precautions as indicated. (2) Blood cultures x3, HIV Ag/Ab and viral load (p24/RNA for acute window), RPR/treponemal serology, hepatitis B/C serologies, EBV/CMV, Bartonella serology. (3) Echocardiography (TTE then TEE) for endocarditis. (4) Imaging: abdominal ultrasound/CT for splenomegaly/abscess; CXR. (5) Empiric antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin +/- ceftriaxone) if endocarditis/sepsis suspected, after cultures. (6) Dermatology assessment of rash; treat syphilis if confirmed. (7) Harm-reduction counselling, addiction/social work referral, and HIV linkage-to-care if positive.

parts_raw.text: What initial empiric antifungal therapy (from 2 different classes) would you use?
What are 3 indications for urgent surgery present in this case.
He is deemed not a candidate for valvular surgery. Based on the 2016 AHA/IDSA guidelines, what is the recommended antifungal management in this case?

questions.model_answer:
a) Initial empiric antifungal therapy combining two classes: (1) a polyene — lipid/liposomal amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg/day), preferably with flucytosine (25 mg/kg/dose QID); PLUS (2) a high-dose echinocandin. Mandell notes amphotericin B plus 5-fluorocytosine and that echinocandins are encouraging for fungal IE.
b) Three indications for urgent surgery present here: (1) Fungal (Candida) endocarditis — infection that cannot be eradicated with antimicrobial therapy alone (ineffective antimicrobial therapy); (2) Severe aortic regurgitation with heart failure (hemodynamic compromise/CHF), the crucial determinant for valve replacement; (3) Large vegetation (13 mm) with systemic embolic phenomena (multiple splenic lesions).
c) When not a surgical candidate: complete the induction course with amphotericin B-based therapy and document clearance of candidemia, then step down (if the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible and the patient is stable) to oral fluconazole 400-800 mg (6-12 mg/kg) daily as long-term/lifelong chronic suppressive therapy because of the high risk of relapse.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific step-down-to-fluconazole and lifelong suppression strategy is from the 2016 AHA IE scientific statement / IDSA Candida guidelines; Mandell confirms only long-term suppressive antifungal therapy in general.

cohort_answer.text: Empiric therapy: Liposomal amphoB (3-5mg/kg) +/- flucytosine; High dose echinocandin. Urgent surgery indications: Fungal endocarditis; Severe heart failure with valve dysfunction; Large mobile vegetation with evidence of embolic phenomena. If not a surgical candidate: Step down therapy to fluconazole 400-800mg daily if susceptible isolates, clinical stability, and cleared bloodstream Candida; for patients who cannot undergo valve replacement, long term suppression with fluconazole 400-800mg daily if isolate susceptible; even with surgery, reasonable to consider lifelong prophylaxis due to recurrence risk

questions.question_raw: Indications for TEE in patient with staph bacteremia and TTE negative (5)

parts.text: List five indications for performing transesophageal echocardiography in a patient with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia and a negative transthoracic echocardiogram.

parts_raw.text: Indications for TEE in patient with staph bacteremia and TTE negative (5)

questions.model_answer: (1) Presence of a prosthetic heart valve or other prosthetic/implanted cardiac material. (2) Presence of an intracardiac device (pacemaker/defibrillator leads). (3) Persistent bacteremia or persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. (4) Clinical or embolic evidence suggesting IE (new regurgitant murmur, new heart failure/conduction abnormality, or embolic/vascular phenomena). (5) Community-acquired SAB or SAB with no removable/identifiable primary focus (and/or the desire to define duration of therapy, e.g., 2 vs 4 weeks). A technically inadequate/non-strictly-negative TTE is itself an indication to proceed to TEE.
questions.beyond_mandell: The discrete list of TEE indications in SAB rests on IDSA/AHA guidance; Mandell supports that TEE is more sensitive than TTE (~95% vs 60-65%), that a negative TTE does not exclude IE, that TEE is preferred with prosthetic valves/complicated IE/perivalvular extension, and that TEE was a cost-effective way to define SAB therapy duration.
